A systematic literature review on algorithm aversion", "abstract": "With the continuing application of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in decision-making, algorithmic decision-making is becoming more efficient, often even outperforming humans. Despite this superior performance, people often consciously or unconsciously display reluctance to rely on algorithms, a phenomenon known as algorithm aversion. Viewed as a behavioral anomaly, algorithm aversion has recently attracted much scholarly attention. With a view to synthesize the findings of existing literature, we systematically review 80 empirical studies identified through searching in seven academic databases and using the snowballing technique. We inductively categorize the influencing factors of algorithm aversion under four main themes: algorithm, individual, task, and high-level. I've drafted the related-work section below. It draws on about 30 papers I found and checked in the database, and I've added notes on gaps and choices at the end. The section is long, so you'll probably want to cut it to fit your paper.

---

## Related Work

### Algorithms often outperform human judgment

Research on trust in algorithms starts from an old finding: in many prediction tasks, formal statistical rules are at least as accurate as expert judgment. Grove et al.'s meta-analysis of "clinical versus mechanical" prediction in human health and behavior found that mechanical methods were on average about 10% more accurate. They substantially beat clinical judgment in 33–47% of studies, while clinicians substantially won in only 6–16% [W2168729696]. This advantage held across task types, kinds of judges, and levels of judge experience, and earlier reviews in clinical psychology reached similar conclusions [W207333959]. Given this record, the behavioral question is why people often fail to use algorithms, and why at other times they rely on them too much.

### Algorithm aversion

Dietvorst, Simmons, and Massey named the phenomenon *algorithm aversion*. In incentivized forecasting tasks, people who had watched an algorithm perform were less confident in it and less likely to choose it over a worse human forecaster. This held even when they had seen the algorithm outperform the human, because people lose confidence in an algorithm faster than in a human after seeing both make the same mistake [W3125633690]. Later work supports the idea that errors are judged unequally. Prahl and Van Swol did not find a general preference for human advice, but after bad advice, use of automated advice fell much more than use of human advice. Participants also said they had more in common with human advisors [W2600700815]. Renier et al. found that errors made by an algorithm triggered harsher gut reactions and stronger behavioral intentions than the same errors made by a human. This was true regardless of the algorithm's maturity, how severe the error was, or the domain [W3167050492].

Aversion does not depend only on seeing errors. Yeomans et al. found that recommender systems predicted which jokes people would find funny better than strangers, friends, or spouses did. People still preferred human recommenders, partly because they thought the human recommendation process was easier to understand [W2913854599]. Applied studies report similar aversion in delegated investing [W4309634305], in investment decisions involving morally controversial companies [W3087513280], and in inventory planning during supply disruptions [W4403540152]. Several systematic reviews organize this literature. Burton et al. group causes and remedies into five themes: expectations and expertise, decision autonomy, incentives, cognitive compatibility, and divergent rationalities [W2981686111]. Mahmud et al. review 80 empirical studies and sort the factors into algorithm, individual, task, and higher-level factors. They note that task and higher-level factors have received relatively little attention [W4200546216].

### Algorithm appreciation and over-reliance

A second line of work shows the opposite pattern. In six experiments, Logg, Minson, and Moore found that lay people followed advice more when they believed it came from an algorithm rather than a person, which they called *algorithm appreciation*. The effect appeared in visual estimates and in forecasts of song popularity and romantic attraction. Notably, researchers asked to predict the outcome expected aversion instead [W2800068874]. You et al. likewise found that people followed algorithmic advice more than identical human advice because they trusted the algorithm more. Telling participants about the algorithm's prediction errors in summary form did not reduce this preference, but a more detailed performance format did [W4281822284]. Bogert et al. found that reliance on algorithmic advice, compared with peer influence, increases as tasks get harder. They also found that inaccurate advice labeled as algorithmic was discounted more strongly [W3152500611].

Appreciation can turn into over-reliance. Banker and Khetani describe *algorithm overdependence*: consumers who believe algorithms have more domain expertise accept algorithmic recommendations even when those recommendations are worse [W4248125493]. This connects to the human-factors concept of automation bias. However, Alon-Barkat and Busuioc found no evidence of automation bias in public-sector decision experiments, including one with civil servants. Instead they found *selective adherence*: people were more likely to follow advice that matched stereotypes, whether it came from an algorithm or a human expert [W4211002924]. Over-reliance may therefore depend on whether advice confirms what people already believe, not only on whether its source is a machine.

### Reconciling aversion and appreciation: moderators

Most recent work treats aversion and appreciation as the outcomes of different conditions rather than as competing claims. Jussupow, Benbasat, and Heinzl argue that the two literatures are hard to integrate because they define and measure the constructs differently. They identify four decision configurations that compare algorithms with human advisors, with the decision-maker's own judgment, or with combinations of these [W4400803056]. This matters because Logg et al.'s appreciation effect weakened when people compared an algorithm with *their own* estimate instead of another person's [W2800068874].

**Framing and perceived competence.** Hou and Jung produced both appreciation and aversion just by changing how the human and the algorithm were described. Perceived expertise mediated the effect, which suggests that some conflicting results in earlier studies come from design choices [W3206874785]. Lay beliefs also matter: consumers who think AI is smarter than humans adopt algorithmic advice more, but only when they see the task as complex [W3193926864].

**Task type.** Lee found that for "mechanical" management tasks, algorithmic and human decisions were seen as equally fair and trustworthy. For tasks requiring "human" skills, algorithmic decisions were seen as less fair and trustworthy because algorithms seem to lack intuition and subjective judgment [W2792183666]. A review of task-specific advice acceptance reaches similar conclusions [W4385299043]. Studies also find more aversion in high-stakes decisions [W4321440879], and some evidence suggests that uncertainty moderates whether people show aversion or appreciation [W4366599035].

**Moral and identity-relevant decisions.** Bigman and Gray found that people do not want machines making moral decisions in driving, law, medicine, or the military. This aversion was mediated by the perception that machines cannot fully think or feel. It persisted even when outcomes were good, and none of the tested remedies removed it [W2886363025]. Jago found that algorithmic work is seen as less morally authentic, so algorithms' moral decisions are judged as less ethical [W2754764889]. In healthcare, Longoni et al. found that resistance to medical AI comes from *uniqueness neglect*, the worry that AI cannot account for a person's unique circumstances. This resistance disappeared when care was framed as personalized, when the decision was for someone else, or when AI supported rather than replaced a physician [W2942858056].

**Expertise and the passage of time.** Experienced forecasters relied on algorithms less than lay people did, and their accuracy suffered as a result [W2800068874]. Turel and Kalhan link initial reliance to implicit prejudice against AI. As people learn how well the algorithm actually performs, this implicit bias carries less weight, which suggests aversion may be temporary [W4391114267]. Other work also looks at whether people recover from aversion over time [W4391904381].

### Interventions that change reliance

The literature also tests ways to reduce aversion. Giving people even a small ability to adjust an algorithm's forecasts made them much more likely to use it and improved their accuracy [W3121705224]. Cheng and Chouldechova only partly replicated this outcome-control effect and pointed to reproducibility problems. They found that letting users choose the training algorithm reduced aversion, but letting them change the inputs did not [W4366547314]. Showing that an algorithm can learn offset the drop in reliance after familiar algorithmic advisors made errors [W3110817755]. Reich et al. found that people avoid algorithms partly because they assume, often wrongly, that algorithms cannot learn from mistakes, and that emphasizing learning ability increases trust [W4283162852].

Transparency has mixed effects. Understanding the process seems to support reliance [W2913854599]. However, Lehmann et al. found that revealing an algorithm that people see as *too simple* sharply reduces use of its advice, while revealing one seen as too complex has no effect [W3189444386]. Detailed performance information can also lower appreciation because of the extra cognitive load [W4281822284].

### Connection to trust in automation

These findings fit a longer tradition in human factors. Lee and See's model of trust in automation holds that people respond to technology socially and that trust guides reliance when systems are too complex to fully understand. The model treats appropriate (calibrated) reliance, rather than maximum reliance, as the goal [W4243342770]. Dzindolet et al. studied how trust affects reliance on automated aids [W2010158189]. Research on automation failure examines how different types of errors shape trust [W2142135351]. Applied to AI, Glikson and Woolley's review distinguishes cognitive trust (driven by tangibility, transparency, reliability, and immediacy) from emotional trust (driven mainly by anthropomorphism). They also note that most evidence comes from short-term, small-sample experiments [W3013998503]. From this perspective, aversion and appreciation are two ways reliance can fail to match an algorithm's actual reliability.

### Summary and gaps

1. Aversion and appreciation coexist. Which one appears depends on the comparison being made (algorithm versus another person or versus oneself), how the advisors are framed, the type of task, how much is at stake, and whether the decision has moral meaning [W4400803056, W3206874785, W2792183666, W2886363025].
2. Seeing errors is a key turning point, but its effect depends on whether people believe the algorithm can learn [W3125633690, W4283162852].
3. Most evidence comes from short online experiments with lay participants. Field and longitudinal studies are scarce [W3013998503, W4200546216].
4. The best target is calibrated reliance, not simply more reliance, given evidence of over-dependence [W4248125493, W4243342770].

- **Next step:** If you tell me your own argument or mechanism, I can rewrite the moderators section so it leads into your contribution.

My study is an online experiment where people choose between advice from an algorithm and advice from a human expert, across tasks that range from forecasting to things that feel more subjective, like predicting which jokes or movies someone will like. In Study 1, two groups of participants were given the same advised point and interval forecasts. One group was told that these were the advice of a human expert and the other that they were generated by a statistical forecasting method. The participants were then asked to adjust forecasts they had previously made in light of this advice. While in both cases the advice led to improved point forecast accuracy and better calibration of the prediction intervals, the advice which apparently emanated from a statistical method was discounted much more severely. When the participants were told that both sources were either human experts or both were statistical methods, the apparent statistical‐based advice had the same influence on the adjusted estimates as the advice that appeared to come from a human expert. text:
I've revised the section. It now opens with the clinical-versus-statistical prediction debate of the 1950s–1990s and gives more space to task type and to studies that compare algorithms with human experts.

Four points from the new searches affect your framing:

- **Meehl already argued the answer depends on the task.** A 1970 review quotes his 1954 thesis: there is no reason to assume formal rules and a clinician's creativity are "equally suited for any given kind of task" [W2129871510]. That gives your design a direct historical starting point.
- **Two studies of subjective tasks disagree, and both match your design.** In Logg et al., people favored algorithmic advice when forecasting song popularity and romantic attraction [W2800068874]. In Yeomans et al., people avoided a recommender that predicted which jokes they'd find funny better than friends or family did [W2913854599]. So subjective tasks alone don't produce aversion, and the section now says so.
- **Algorithm versus expert is not the same comparison as algorithm versus self.** Appreciation weakens when the alternative is the person's own judgment [W2800068874]. Studies that use a human expert as the comparison have found aversion [W2158570360, W2070125214]. I've treated this as its own moderator.
- **Castelo et al. (2019, "Task-dependent algorithm aversion") is not in the database.** It's probably the closest earlier work to your study, since it varies how subjective tasks seem. Dietvorst & Bharti (2020) and Meehl's 1954 book are also missing. I've marked where each one belongs; please check them yourself before citing.

---

## Related Work

### Origins: the clinical–statistical debate

The question of whether to rely on formulas or on human judgment is much older than the term "algorithm aversion." It began in clinical psychology as the *clinical-versus-statistical* (or actuarial) prediction debate, made famous by Meehl's 1954 book. Meehl framed it as a question about tasks. He argued there was no reason to assume that "explicitly formalized mathematical rules and the clinician's creativity are equally suited for any given kind of task," or that their relative performance is the same across tasks [W2129871510]. The evidence that followed mostly favored the formula. Grove and Meehl reviewed 136 studies across many prediction targets. They concluded that mechanical prediction was "almost invariably equal to or superior to" clinical judgment, with roots going back to a 1928 parole-prediction study that combined 21 objective factors [W2102256472]. A later meta-analysis found mechanical prediction about 10% more accurate on average. Clinicians substantially beat the formula in only 6–16% of studies, and the advantage held regardless of task, judge type, or judge experience [W2168729696]. Dawes showed that even *improper* linear models, such as ones with equal weights, beat clinical intuition when numerical outcomes are predicted from numerical inputs [W2056418346]. In business forecasting, Blattberg and Hoch found that combining a simple model with managerial judgment beat either one alone, and proposed a "50% model + 50% manager" rule [W2104546629].

This early literature already recorded people's reluctance to use these methods, as distinct from their accuracy. Dawes listed technical, psychological, and ethical "resistances" to letting linear models make important social decisions [W2056418346]. Grove and Meehl discussed reasons for "widespread resistance" to the comparative evidence [W2102256472]. A review of the debate concluded that actuarial methods "are rarely employed in practice for a variety of reasons" [W207333959]. Armstrong's "seer-sucker theory" described the same pattern among people who pay for expert forecasts despite evidence that the experts add little value [W2137384635]. In personnel selection, Highhouse traced resistance to decision aids to two beliefs: that near-perfect prediction is possible, and that experience improves intuitive prediction of human behavior [W2171321543]. Lay participants likewise judged holistic combination of interview and test scores to be better than mechanical combination [W1522638407].

Early experiments began comparing advice from a computer with advice from a human expert directly, the setup most similar to modern studies. Patients were more likely to follow a surgeon's recommendation than the same recommendation from a computer program, and trusted the physician more. Following a physician also reduced their feeling of responsibility more than following a computer [W2070125214]. In stock-price forecasting, identical advice was discounted much more when labeled as coming from a statistical method than from a human expert, but only when both sources were shown together [W2158570360]. Physicians who used a computerized diagnostic aid were rated less favorably than physicians who diagnosed unaided. Physicians who consulted a human colleague were not rated lower, which suggests the penalty is specific to non-human tools [W2085105383]. Human-factors research on trust in automation developed alongside this work. It studied how trust shapes reliance on automated aids [W2010158189] and argued that the goal is *appropriate* reliance, matched to how reliable the system actually is [W4243342770].

### Algorithm aversion

Dietvorst, Simmons, and Massey named the effect *algorithm aversion*. In incentivized forecasting tasks, people who had seen an algorithm perform were less likely to bet on it than on a worse human forecaster, even after seeing it outperform the human. The reason was that confidence in algorithms dropped faster after the same mistake [W3125633690]. This unequal response to errors has been replicated in several ways. Prahl and Van Swol did not find a baseline preference for human advisors, but use of automated advice fell more steeply after bad advice [W2600700815]. In an 18-day field study, inaccurate algorithms were penalized more than inaccurate humans; the penalty was strongest at first and faded over time [W4206941179]. Algorithmic errors also produced harsher emotional and behavioral reactions across different levels of algorithm maturity, error severity, and domain [W3167050492].

Aversion also appears in preference prediction, the kind of subjective task in your design. Yeomans et al. found that a recommender system predicted which jokes people would find funny better than strangers, friends, or spouses did. People still preferred human recommenders, partly because the human process felt easier to understand [W2913854599]. In the movie domain, MovieLens collaborative filtering outperformed human recommenders on average, though some individuals beat it substantially [W2075329139]. In subjective preference tasks, then, algorithms can be accurate and still unwanted. Systematic reviews organize the proposed causes of aversion around expectations and expertise, decision autonomy, incentives, cognitive compatibility, and divergent rationalities [W2981686111], or around factors related to the algorithm, the individual, the task, and higher-level context. The task and higher-level categories have been studied least [W4200546216].

### Algorithm appreciation

A second line of research reports the opposite. In six experiments, Logg, Minson, and Moore found that lay people followed advice more when it was labeled as coming from an algorithm than from a person. This *algorithm appreciation* appeared in visual estimation and also in forecasting song popularity and romantic attraction, which are fairly subjective domains. Researchers asked to predict the result expected aversion [W2800068874]. You et al. found that people followed algorithmic advice more than identical human advice because they trusted the algorithm more. Telling them about the algorithm's errors in summary form did not remove this preference [W4281822284]. Reliance on algorithmic advice, compared with peer advice, grows as tasks get harder [W3152500611]. Appreciation can also become over-reliance: consumers who believe algorithms have more expertise follow algorithmic recommendations even when they are worse [W4248125493]. Not all studies find this. Public-sector experiments found no general automation bias, only a tendency to follow advice that matched stereotypes, whether it came from an algorithm or a human expert [W4211002924].

### What makes people more or less willing to rely on algorithms

**Task type: objective versus subjective.** Meehl's view that suitability depends on the task [W2129871510] is now mostly studied as a question of people's *perceptions* of the task. Lee found that algorithmic decisions were judged as fair and trustworthy as human decisions for "mechanical" managerial tasks. For tasks requiring "human" skills, they were judged less fair and less trustworthy, because algorithms seemed to lack intuition and subjective judgment [W2792183666]. Jin and Li found that consumers trusted algorithms more in less unstructured tasks, mediated by perceived accuracy, and trusted humans more in highly unstructured tasks, mediated by perceived flexibility [W4415545653]. Reviews of task-specific advice acceptance reach similar conclusions [W4385299043], and creative tasks have been proposed as a likely boundary condition for appreciation [W3046553882]. In the most extreme case, moral decisions, aversion is strong and hard to reverse. It is mediated by the perception that machines cannot fully think or feel [W2886363025], and by judgments that algorithmic work is less authentic [W2754764889]. In medicine, aversion comes from *uniqueness neglect*, the worry that AI cannot account for an individual's particular circumstances. It disappears when the AI is presented as personalized or as supporting a physician rather than replacing one [W2942858056]. The conflict between Logg et al.'s appreciation in subjective forecasts [W2800068874] and Yeomans et al.'s aversion in joke recommendations [W2913854599] suggests that a task being subjective is not enough to predict aversion. Perceived subjectivity may interact with other factors, such as whose preferences are being predicted or how the advisors are described. [*Add Castelo et al., 2019, here once checked.*]

**Who the algorithm is compared against.** Many conflicting findings come from differences in study design. Jussupow et al. distinguish decision configurations in which algorithms are compared with a human advisor, with the participant's own judgment, or with combinations of both [W4400803056]. Appreciation weakened when people chose between an algorithm and their *own* estimate [W2800068874]. Early studies that used human *experts* as the comparison found aversion [W2070125214, W2158570360]. Hou and Jung produced both appreciation and aversion just by changing how the human and the algorithm were described, with perceived expertise as the mediator [W3206874785].

**Performance information and experience.** Seeing errors increases aversion [W3125633690, W2600700815], but evidence that the algorithm can learn offsets this [W3110817755, W4283162852]. The penalty for inaccurate algorithms fades over repeated interactions [W4206941179]. Implicit prejudice against AI shapes reliance at first, and its influence shrinks as performance information builds up [W4391114267].

**Individual differences.** Experienced forecasters relied on algorithms less than lay people and lost accuracy as a result [W2800068874]. This fits the early "myth of expertise" account [W2171321543]. Believing that AI is smarter than humans increases adoption, but only for tasks seen as complex [W3193926864]. People with a stronger internal locus of control (the belief that they control their own outcomes) judge decisions made with a computer aid more negatively [W2085105383].

**Design interventions.** Letting people make even small adjustments to an algorithm's output increases its use [W3121705224]. A replication supported this only partly, and found that letting users choose the training algorithm also helps [W4366547314]. Transparency can backfire if it makes an algorithm look simpler than people expected [W3189444386], or if detailed performance information adds too much cognitive load [W4281822284].

### Summary

The resistance seen in the clinical–statistical debate and the modern contrast between aversion and appreciation are best understood as depending on conditions, not as a single bias. The evidence points to four main moderators: perceived task subjectivity, the comparison advisor (a human expert, a peer, or oneself), how the advisors are framed, and the decision-maker's beliefs and experience. Few studies vary task subjectivity across a range of tasks while keeping the alternative fixed as a human expert, which is the comparison your design makes. # Related Work

### Origins: the clinical–statistical debate

The question of whether to rely on formulas or on human judgment is much older than the term "algorithm aversion." It began in clinical psychology as the debate over *clinical versus statistical* (actuarial) prediction, made prominent by Meehl's 1954 book [*cite Meehl, 1954*]. Meehl framed it as a question about tasks. He argued there was "no convincing reason to assume that explicitly formalized mathematical rules and the clinician's creativity are equally suited for any given kind of task," or that their relative performance is the same across tasks [W2129871510]. The evidence that followed mostly favored the formula. Dawes, Faust, and Meehl summarized this research in *Science*: the actuarial method was more accurate, yet professionals resisted the findings [W2012218966]. Grove and Meehl reviewed 136 studies across a wide range of prediction targets. They concluded that mechanical prediction was "almost invariably equal to or superior to" clinical judgment, with roots going back to a 1928 parole-prediction study that combined 21 objective factors [W2102256472]. A later meta-analysis found mechanical prediction about 10% more accurate on average. Clinicians were substantially more accurate in only 6–16% of studies, and the advantage held regardless of task, type of judge, or judge experience [W2168729696]. Dawes showed that even *improper* linear models, such as ones with equal weights, beat clinical intuition when numerical outcomes are predicted from numerical inputs [W2056418346]. In business forecasting, Blattberg and Hoch found that combining a simple model with managerial judgment beat either one alone, and proposed a "50% model + 50% manager" rule [W2104546629].

This literature also documented reluctance to *use* these methods, as distinct from their accuracy. Dawes listed technical, psychological, and ethical "resistances" to letting linear models make important social decisions [W2056418346], and Grove and Meehl discussed reasons for "widespread resistance" to the comparative evidence [W2102256472]. A review of the debate concluded that actuarial methods "are rarely employed in practice for a variety of reasons" [W207333959]. Armstrong's "seer-sucker theory" described a similar willingness to pay for expert forecasts despite little evidence of their value [W2137384635]. Studies of lay attitudes confirmed that this resistance is common. In legal and medical scenarios, students and community members rated clinical strategies above actuarial ones on preference, perceived accuracy, fairness, and ethicalness. They also rated fully rational strategies above heuristic ones, so an actuarial strategy built on a simple heuristic was rated lowest of all [W2150479185]. In personnel selection, Highhouse traced resistance to decision aids to two beliefs: that near-perfect prediction is possible, and that experience improves intuitive prediction (a "myth of expertise") [W2171321543]. Lay participants likewise judged holistic combination of interview and test scores to be better than mechanical combination [W1522638407].

Early experiments also compared advice from a computer with advice from a human expert directly, the comparison closest to modern work. Patients were more likely to follow a physician's recommendation than the same recommendation from a computer program. They trusted the physician more, and following the physician reduced their feeling of responsibility more [W2070125214]. In stock-price forecasting, identical advice was discounted much more when labeled as coming from a statistical method than from a human expert, but only when both sources were shown together [W2158570360]. Physicians who used a computerized diagnostic aid were rated less favorably than physicians who diagnosed unaided. Physicians who consulted a human colleague were not rated lower, which suggests the penalty is specific to non-human tools [W2085105383]. Human-factors research on trust in automation developed alongside this work. It argues that trust guides reliance when systems are too complex to understand fully, and that the goal is *appropriate* reliance, matched to how reliable the system actually is [W4243342770].

### Algorithm aversion and algorithm appreciation: two foundational studies

Two studies anchor the current debate, and their results are less contradictory than they first look. Dietvorst, Simmons, and Massey ran five studies in which participants saw forecasts from an algorithm, a human, both, or neither. Participants then chose whether to tie their incentives to the algorithm's or the human's future forecasts [W3125633690]. Those who had *seen the algorithm perform* were less confident in it and less likely to choose it over a worse human forecaster. This held even among participants who had watched the algorithm outperform the human. The authors attribute this *algorithm aversion* to unequal reactions to errors: people "more quickly lose confidence in algorithmic than human forecasters after seeing them make the same mistake" [W3125633690].

Logg, Minson, and Moore, in contrast, found across six experiments that lay participants "adhere more to advice when they think it comes from an algorithm than from a person." The effect appeared in numeric estimates about a visual stimulus and in forecasts of song popularity and romantic attraction. Researchers asked to predict the result expected the opposite [W2800068874]. This *algorithm appreciation* held whether advice was shown jointly or separately. It weakened under two conditions: when people chose between an algorithm's estimate and *their own* rather than another advisor's, and when participants had forecasting expertise. Experienced professionals relied on algorithmic advice less than lay people did, and their accuracy suffered as a result [W2800068874].

The studies differ in at least three ways that may explain the opposite results. First, *performance information*: Dietvorst et al. found aversion mainly after participants had seen the algorithm perform and err. Logg et al.'s participants appear to have judged the advisor before seeing any results. Second, *the outcome measured*: Dietvorst et al. asked for an all-or-nothing choice of which forecaster to tie payment to. Logg et al. measured how much people adhered to advice when forming their own estimate, following the judge-advisor approach [W2032056105, W2020463305]. Third, *the comparison*: Logg et al. show directly that appreciation shrinks when the alternative is the participant's own judgment rather than an external advisor's [W2800068874]. Results therefore depend on who the human alternative is in each design. Read together, the studies fit an account in which people start with a favorable view of algorithms and then penalize algorithmic errors more than human errors. Later work supports this. Prahl and Van Swol found no general preference for human advice, but reliance on automation dropped more steeply after bad advice [W2600700815]. A longitudinal field study found that inaccurate algorithms were penalized more than inaccurate humans, with the penalty strongest early on and fading over time [W4206941179].

### Further evidence of aversion

Other studies extend the error-based account. Algorithmic errors produce harsher emotional and behavioral reactions than equivalent human errors, regardless of the algorithm's maturity, the severity of the error, or the domain [W3167050492]. Aversion also appears in preference prediction, where errors are not the explanation. Yeomans et al. found that a recommender system predicted which jokes people would find funny better than strangers, friends, or spouses did. People still preferred human recommenders, partly because the human process felt easier to understand [W2913854599]. In the movie domain, MovieLens collaborative filtering outperformed human recommenders on average, though some individuals beat it substantially [W2075329139]. Applied studies report aversion in delegated investing [W4309634305], in investment decisions involving morally controversial companies [W3087513280], and in operational planning during disruptions [W4403540152]. Systematic reviews group the proposed causes into expectations and expertise, decision autonomy, incentives, cognitive compatibility, and divergent rationalities [W2981686111]. Another review sorts them into factors related to the algorithm, the individual, the task, and higher-level context, and notes that task and higher-level factors are the least studied [W4200546216].

### Further evidence of appreciation and over-reliance

Appreciation has also been replicated and extended. You et al. found that people followed algorithmic advice more than identical human advice because they trusted the algorithm more. Telling them about the algorithm's prediction errors in summary form did not remove this preference, although a more detailed format did reduce it [W4281822284]. Reliance on algorithmic advice, compared with peer advice, grows as tasks get harder [W3152500611]. Appreciation can become over-reliance: consumers who believe algorithms have more domain expertise follow algorithmic recommendations even when those recommendations are worse [W4248125493]. The evidence for a general automation bias is mixed, however. Public-sector experiments, including one with civil servants, found no general tendency to over-rely on algorithmic advice. They found instead that people adhered more to advice that matched stereotypes, whether it came from an algorithm or a human expert [W4211002924].

### What makes people more or less willing to rely on algorithms

Most recent work treats aversion and appreciation as outcomes of different conditions rather than as competing claims. Jussupow, Benbasat, and Heinzl argue that the two literatures have been hard to integrate because they define and measure the constructs differently. They distinguish decision configurations in which algorithms are compared with human advisors, with the decision-maker's own judgment, or with combinations of these [W4400803056]. The literature points to the following moderators.

**Task type: objective versus subjective.** Meehl's view that suitability depends on the task [W2129871510] is now mostly studied as a question of how people *perceive* the task. Lee found that algorithmic decisions were judged as fair and trustworthy as human decisions for "mechanical" managerial tasks. For tasks requiring "human" skills, they were judged less fair and less trustworthy, because algorithms seemed to lack intuition and subjective judgment [W2792183666]. Jin and Li found that consumers trusted algorithms more in less unstructured tasks, mediated by perceived accuracy. In highly unstructured tasks they trusted humans more, mediated by perceived flexibility [W4415545653]. A review of task-specific advice acceptance reaches similar conclusions [W4385299043]. [*Add Castelo et al., 2019, "Task-dependent algorithm aversion," here once checked.*] In the most extreme case, moral decisions, aversion is strong and hard to reverse. It is mediated by the perception that machines cannot fully think or feel [W2886363025], and by judgments that algorithmic work is less authentic [W2754764889]. In medicine, aversion comes from *uniqueness neglect*, the worry that AI cannot account for an individual's particular circumstances. It disappears when AI care is presented as personalized or as supporting rather than replacing a physician [W2942858056]. The subjective-task evidence is inconsistent, however. Logg et al. found appreciation when people forecast song popularity and romantic attraction [W2800068874], whereas Yeomans et al. found aversion to joke recommendations [W2913854599]. A task being subjective is therefore not enough to predict aversion. Its effect may depend on other factors, such as whose preferences are being predicted, how the advisors are described, and what the alternative advisor is.

**Who the algorithm is compared against and how it is framed.** Appreciation weakens when the alternative is the participant's own judgment [W2800068874]. Studies that used human *experts* as the alternative have often found aversion [W2070125214, W2158570360]. Hou and Jung produced both appreciation and aversion just by changing how the human and the algorithm were described, with perceived expertise as the mediator [W3206874785]. Lay beliefs matter in the same way: people who believe AI is smarter than humans adopt algorithmic advice more, but only when they see the task as complex [W3193926864].

**Performance information and experience.** Seeing errors increases aversion [W3125633690, W2600700815]. Evidence that an algorithm can learn offsets this [W3110817755], and emphasizing learning ability corrects the mistaken belief that algorithms cannot learn from mistakes [W4283162852]. Implicit prejudice against AI shapes reliance at first, and its influence shrinks as performance information builds up [W4391114267]. The penalty for inaccurate algorithms also fades over repeated interactions [W4206941179].

**Individual differences.** Domain expertise reduces reliance on algorithms [W2800068874], consistent with the "myth of expertise" account [W2171321543]. People with a stronger internal locus of control, the belief that they control their own outcomes, judge decisions made with a computer aid more negatively [W2085105383].

**Design interventions.** Letting people make even small adjustments to an algorithm's output substantially increases its use and improves accuracy [W3121705224]. A replication supported this only partly, and found that letting users choose the training algorithm also reduces aversion [W4366547314]. Transparency has mixed effects. Understanding the recommendation process supports reliance [W2913854599], but revealing an algorithm that seems too simple reduces use of its advice [W3189444386]. This matches the low ratings people give heuristic actuarial strategies [W2150479185]. Detailed performance information can also lower appreciation by adding cognitive load [W4281822284].

### Summary and positioning

Across seven decades, the evidence shows that formal methods often outperform human judgment and that people often resist them. Recent work shows that this resistance depends on conditions. The default tendency can favor algorithms [W2800068874], but it changes after algorithms are seen to err [W3125633690, W2600700815]. It also changes with perceived task subjectivity [W2792183666, W4415545653], with whether the alternative is the decision-maker or an external expert [W2800068874, W2158570360], with how the advisors are framed [W3206874785], and with the decision-maker's expertise and beliefs [W2171321543, W3193926864]. Evidence on subjective tasks is especially mixed [W2800068874, W2913854599]. Few studies vary task subjectivity across a range of tasks while keeping the alternative fixed as a human expert. Our design does this: participants choose between an algorithm and a human expert across tasks ranging from forecasting to preference prediction.
